Duplication analysis

Source: vignettes/duplicates.Rmd
duplicates.Rmd

Repeated values in a dataset can be a sign of copied or fabricated data. scrutiny has three functions for counting duplicates, each with an audit() method for summaries. The examples use the pigs4 dataset:

pigs4
#> # A tibble: 5 × 3
#>   snout  tail wings
#>   <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>
#> 1  4.73  6.88  6.09
#> 2  8.13  7.33  8.27
#> 3  4.22  5.17  4.4 
#> 4  4.22  7.57  5.92
#> 5  5.17  8.13  5.17

Frequency tabulation with duplicate_count()

A good first step is a frequency table:

pigs4 |>
  duplicate_count()
#> # A tibble: 11 × 4
#>    value frequency locations          locations_n
#>    <chr>     <int> <chr>                    <int>
#>  1 5.17          3 snout, tail, wings           3
#>  2 4.22          2 snout                        1
#>  3 8.13          2 snout, tail                  2
#>  4 4.73          1 snout                        1
#>  5 6.88          1 tail                         1
#>  6 7.33          1 tail                         1
#>  7 7.57          1 tail                         1
#>  8 4.4           1 wings                        1
#>  9 5.92          1 wings                        1
#> 10 6.09          1 wings                        1
#> 11 8.27          1 wings                        1

Each distinct value is one row, ordered by its frequency. locations names the columns in which the value appears, and locations_n counts them. For example, 5.17 appears 3 times, once each in snout, tail, and wings, so locations_n is 3. 4.22 appears twice, but both times in snout, so locations_n is 1.

audit() summarizes frequency and locations_n:

pigs4 |>
  duplicate_count() |>
  audit()
#> # A tibble: 2 × 8
#>   term         mean    sd median   min   max na_count na_rate
#>   <chr>       <dbl> <dbl>  <int> <int> <int>    <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 frequency    1.36 0.674      1     1     3        0       0
#> 2 locations_n  1.27 0.647      1     1     3        0       0

Counting by column pair with duplicate_count_colpair()

A sequence of values may be repeated across columns. duplicate_count_colpair() compares every pair of columns:

pigs4 |>
  duplicate_count_colpair()
#> # A tibble: 3 × 7
#>   x     y     count total_x total_y rate_x rate_y
#>   <chr> <chr> <int>   <int>   <int>  <dbl>  <dbl>
#> 1 snout tail      2       5       5    0.4    0.4
#> 2 snout wings     1       5       5    0.2    0.2
#> 3 tail  wings     1       5       5    0.2    0.2

count is the number of values of x that also appear in y. total_x and total_y are the numbers of non-missing values in each column, rate_x is the proportion of x values that also appear in y, and rate_y the proportion of y values that also appear in x. Without missing values, total_x equals total_y, and rate_x equals rate_y unless a value repeats within a column.

Here, snout and tail overlap the most: 2 of their 5 values are the same, a rate of 0.4. Summarize with audit():

pigs4 |>
  duplicate_count_colpair() |>
  audit()
#> # A tibble: 5 × 8
#>   term     mean    sd median   min   max na_count na_rate
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>  <dbl> <dbl> <dbl>    <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 count   1.33  0.577    1     1     2          0       0
#> 2 total_x 5     0        5     5     5          0       0
#> 3 total_y 5     0        5     5     5          0       0
#> 4 rate_x  0.267 0.115    0.2   0.2   0.4        0       0
#> 5 rate_y  0.267 0.115    0.2   0.2   0.4        0       0

Counting by observation with duplicate_tally()

duplicate_tally() keeps the shape of the data. Next to each column, it adds one ending in _n that counts how often each value appears in the data frame as a whole:

pigs4 |>
  duplicate_tally()
#> # A tibble: 5 × 6
#>   snout snout_n tail  tail_n wings wings_n
#>   <chr>   <int> <chr>  <int> <chr>   <int>
#> 1 4.73        1 6.88       1 6.09        1
#> 2 8.13        2 7.33       1 8.27        1
#> 3 4.22        2 5.17       3 4.4         1
#> 4 4.22        2 7.57       1 5.92        1
#> 5 5.17        3 8.13       2 5.17        3

For example, 4.22 appears twice, both times in snout, so both of its entries in snout_n are 2. 8.13 appears once in snout and once in tail, so both of its entries are 2 as well.

audit() summarizes each _n column, and all of them together in the ".total" row:

pigs4 |>
  duplicate_tally() |>
  audit()
#> # A tibble: 4 × 8
#>   term     mean    sd median   min   max na_count na_rate
#>   <chr>   <dbl> <dbl>  <int> <int> <int>    <int>   <dbl>
#> 1 snout_n  2    0.707      2     1     3        0       0
#> 2 tail_n   1.6  0.894      1     1     3        0       0
#> 3 wings_n  1.4  0.894      1     1     3        0       0
#> 4 .total   1.67 0.816      1     1     3        0       0
